title: 7 ways to improve travel policy compliance
summary: Employees break travel policy when it's long, hard to find, or slower than booking on their own. Seven practical fixes that keep trips in policy after launch.
body_markdown:
Definition


**What is travel policy compliance?** Travel policy compliance is the share of business trips booked through your approved channel and within your policy's rules on fares, hotels, and approvals. A trip booked on a personal card or over the hotel cap counts against it, even when the traveler had a good reason.


Four months ago, you launched a travel program. The booking tool is live, the policy is written, but trips still come in on personal cards, with hotels over the cap and receipts arriving weeks later.


Knowing how to improve travel policy compliance starts with one idea: make the in-policy option the fastest and easiest way to book. Out-of-policy trips often happen because the rules are hard to find, or because the approved channel is slower than someone booking on their own.


Seven small changes can make in-policy the easier choice, and none of them needs a travel manager or a stricter policy.


## Key takeaways


- Employees book out of policy when the compliant path is slower or harder to find than booking on their own.
- Almost a third (32%) of travel buyers say employees break policy because they haven't read or aren't familiar with the rules, and 51% of policies run longer than ten pages (GBTA, 2026).
- In Expensify Travel, you can limit what travelers see to in-policy options, and every booking is recorded as an expense automatically.
- Enforce the rules when people book, while there's still time to pick a different flight or hotel.
- Track one number, the share of trips booked in channel, and share it by team.


## 1. Make booking work on a phone


Plenty of trips get booked in the back of an Uber or between meetings. If your[corporate travel booking tool](https://use.expensify.com/blog/corporate-travel-booking-tool) only works on a laptop, the airline's app is going to win.


Pick a tool that lets travelers book flights, hotels, rail, and car rentals from their phone, and change a trip there too. When the approved channel is also the fastest one on the road, people use it without being told.


Test this yourself before you roll it out. Book a one-night trip on your phone, then change the return flight, and time how long both take. If it's slower than booking directly with the airline, your travelers will notice before you do.

## 2. Show only in-policy options


If a $600 hotel appears next to a $220 hotel in search results, someone will pick it and explain later.


Set your booking tool to show only options that fit the policy, or at least put them first and flag anything outside the rules with a clear note on why. That moves travel policy enforcement from the month-end audit to the moment of booking, when the traveler can still choose something else.


In GBTA's 2026 travel policy survey, 35% of travel managers named[booking outside required channels as the single largest compliance issue](https://gbta.org/corporate-travel-policies-strengthen-modernize-and-embrace-ai%E2%94%80while-opportunities-remain-for-improving-accessibility-policy-clarity-and-compliance/) . When a travel booking tool does the filtering, travelers find the right options in one place and have less reason to shop around.


## 3. Cut the policy to one page


Nobody reads a 30-page travel policy before booking a flight to Denver. They skim it once, if that, and guess the rest.


In the same GBTA survey, 51% of travel policies ran longer than ten pages, and almost a third (32%) of travel buyers said employees break policy because they haven't read or aren't familiar with the rules.


Put the rules people need on one page, like the cabin class, the hotel cap, what needs approval, and how to get help. Keep the detail in an appendix for the rare questions. For a starting point, see how to write a[travel expense policy employees will actually read](https://use.expensify.com/resource-center/guides/travel-expense-policy-employees-will-actually-read-plus-free-template) .


## 4. Ask for approval only where it changes the decision


If your managers have to sign off on every train ticket, approvals turn into a rubber stamp, and travelers will start booking around them to save time.


Save pre-approval for the trips where a manager might actually say no, such as international travel, trips over a set amount, or anything outside the usual cabin or hotel rules. Everything else can book straight through, since the policy is already built into the search results.


When approval is needed, set a turnaround time and a backup approver. A request that sits for two days while fares climb teaches people to skip the process next time. The guide to[travel and expense policy best practices](https://use.expensify.com/resource-center/guides/travel-and-expense-policy-best-practices-with-expensify) covers approval options, from automatic approval with a review window to a hard yes or no.


## 5. Make help one message away


Flights get canceled, meetings move, and hotels lose reservations. When plans change, people book wherever is fastest, and that's usually not your booking tool.


Make sure your travelers can reach an actual human quickly when something goes wrong, without leaving the approved channel. A rebooking handled by an agent stays on the same trip as the original booking, with no second trip fee.


With[Expensify Travel](https://use.expensify.com/travel) , travelers can reach a travel agent by chat, phone, or email. Self-serve trips cost $15 per trip, with no fee to change them yourself. A trip booked or changed by an agent costs $25, charged once per trip no matter how many changes. Tell travelers about the agent option before their first trip, so they know who to turn to when on a business trip.


## 6. Put the expense on autopilot


Business travel policy compliance doesn't end when the traveler gets home. A trip that's booked in policy but expensed three weeks late still leaves you chasing receipts at month-end.


Fix that by making every booking turn into an expense on its own. When the receipt is generated from the booking and lands on a trip report automatically, there's nothing for the traveler to forward and nothing for you to chase.


It also makes the policy easier to follow, since the expense already carries the right category and matches what was approved. Out-of-pocket costs like taxis and meals still need receipts, but flights and hotels are handled.


See how[travel expense reimbursement](https://use.expensify.com/travel-expense-reimbursement) works when bookings and expenses live in one place.


## 7. Track one number and share it by team


You can measure corporate travel policy compliance a dozen ways, but the first item on this list tells you most of what you need. It's the share of trips booked in channel, out of all trips taken, including the ones reimbursed after the fact.


Track it every month and report it by team instead of by person. Team-level numbers show where the policy or the tool isn't working, without turning compliance into a list of names.


When one team's number drops, talk to them. The reason is often a route the tool doesn't cover well, a hotel the team always uses, or an approval that took too long.
